1.pericope_label: Tola of Issachar and Jair the Gileadite: two quiet judgeships

schools.summary: Open with the difficulty that quiet and peaceable reigns, best to live in, are worst to write of, yielding least variety for a historian; call the tribe of the first judge one disposed to serve, since its patriarch bowed his shoulder to bear, and find it the more remarkable that one of it is raised to rule, those who humble themselves being exalted; note that his name signifies a worm but was his ancestor's and so no shame to him; explain his settling outside his own tribe by the convenience of suitors, the place lying more in the heart of the country; and read the second judge's Gileadite origin as God's care that the remote tribes should share the honour of government while it shifted from tribe to tribe.

Deny that the phrase implies the usurper had defended anyone, he being no judge of God's raising up but one who left the people in idolatry, and take the new judge for a happy instrument of composing the dissensions he had caused, recovering them from idolatry and protecting their liberties; and take the riding of the sons for a mark of honour, supposing them appointed under their father to do justice in the several parts of the country.

State the problem that nothing has been said of any oppression, refuse the assumption that the people had been constantly harassed by neighbours, and hold that the judge delivered them even if he only regulated the affairs of the tribes that acknowledged him and kept the nation from falling back into idolatry; limit his jurisdiction to the northern and perhaps eastern tribes, the southern ones having taken no part in the earlier war; find a concession in the very phrase there arose, which implies a less direct call than is used of other judges; allow that the usurper, though not counted among the judges, may have kept foreign enemies in check,; call the tribe indolent, note that it furnished no other judge, and connect the names with the trade in purple dyes; see an ostentatious polygamy in the thirty sons and note that the horse was little used in the country till much later; and hear the pun on the judge's name, the ass colts and the cities, the last purposely altered for the play, adding that such wordplay points to a very early literature and that the Greek euphemism happily preserved it.

Reason from the silence, that since the first judge held office twenty-three years after those troubles the land is likely to have had rest, no enemy making hostile incursions during his presidency and his successor's, which together ran forty-five years; and take the sons riding on ass colts for persons of consideration keeping up a dignity in their departments, inferring prosperity from a man able to give a village to each of thirty sons.

debates: What the first judge delivered Israel from, when no oppression has been mentioned.
What character belonged to the tribe of Issachar.
Whether the thirty sons on their ass colts indicate office or display.
What the wordplay in the fourth verse implies about the age of the narrative.
outliers: Ellicott alone allows that Abimelech may nevertheless have kept foreign enemies in check.
Ellicott alone connects the two Issachar names with the trade in purple dyes, and alone notes that the Greek euphemism accidentally preserved the pun.
Clarke alone infers from the silence of the record that the land had rest for forty-five years together.
Henry alone explains the judge's move to Mount Ephraim by the convenience of those who came to him for judgment.
Keil alone restricts the judgeship to the northern and eastern tribes.

5.pericope_label: The death of Jair, the seven strange gods, and eighteen years of oppression

schools.summary: Weigh the rival sites for the burial place, preferring the city of Gilead to the village six miles from Megiddo on the ground that they are not the same place, and identify it with the town listed among the cities of Peraea taken by Antiochus; say that nothing is more provoking to God than idolatry; and supply three answers where the text names no year — the year the last judge died, the first year of the bondage, or a reading that takes the phrase as from that year onward.

Count seven deities and set them against the seven nations from whose hands the people had been delivered, calling the correspondence unmistakeable, since the tale of idols was balanced against the tale of deliverances and so filled up the measure of iniquity; illustrate the whole catalogue out of English verse, on the ground that the poet drew his details from a learned treatise on the Syrian gods; declare the narrative evidently imperfect where no year is specified; find an assonance in the pair of verbs for vexing and oppressing; and gloss the opening clause literally as added to do evil, joining new sins to the old.

Number five nations and pair each with its deity, explaining that they are called gods in the plural because their images and places of worship were multiplied through the land; and settle the geography of the double oppression, the one nation lying west of Jordan and the other east, joined for the occasion though the eastern was the more active.

Treat the apostasy as a blunder as well as a sin: it looks as if the chief trade of the nation had been to import deities from all countries, and it is hard to say whether that was more impious or impolitic, since no nation with any sense of honour changed its gods, much wealth must have gone out in offerings to the mother temples abroad, and the priests of those deities would follow in crowds and take root, so that strangers devoured their strength; observe that those courted for friendship became enemies, a man being punished in the thing wherein he offends; note that they did not even admit their own God among the many, since those who think to serve both God and Mammon will soon forsake God, and if God have not all the heart he will soon have none of it; and read the double oppression as two millstones, which is what the word rendered oppressed actually says.

debates: Where the second judge was buried.
How many deities are listed here, and whether the number carries a meaning.
Whether the unspecified year is a defect in the record or can be determined.
What Israel gained or lost by importing the worship of its neighbours.
outliers: Henry alone reads the idolatry as an economic and political miscalculation as well as an offence.
Ellicott alone illustrates the catalogue of deities from English poetry, justifying it by the poet's own learned source.
Ellicott alone calls the notice of the year defective, where Gill alone supplies three solutions for it.
Clarke alone counts five nations with their gods where the others count seven deities.
Keil and Ellicott independently match the seven idols to the seven deliverances.

9.pericope_label: The cry of Israel, and the Lord's answer out of the record of past deliverances

schools.summary: Set out the candidates for the messenger — a prophet, as two rabbis hold, or the one a third names, who could not have been living then; a created angel; or the uncreated one appearing in human form; affirm the oppression by nations of whom no record survives, since they were left in the land to distress Israel and the thing is not to be questioned though no mention of it remains; and describe how the invaders, not content with the oppression beyond Jordan, crossed over to subdue the tribes that lay readiest.
Leave the manner of the reproof open, since by what means it was conveyed we know not, and it must have been by an angel, a prophet, or some holy man inspired for the occasion.

Take the confession as that of a malefactor upon the rack and of a child under the rod, noting that the omissions are confessed first, since in these the sin began, and the commissions after; be unable to decide between the angel of the earlier chapter and the prophet of the later; observe that it was kind of God to notice the cry at all, and kinder to send, when they began to repent, a message fit to increase repentance and prepare them for deliverance; reduce the reproof to the sentence that they forsook him who brought them out of their troubles and served gods who brought them into them, forsaking their own mercies for their own delusions; and put their folly in commercial terms, that they had been at vast expense to obtain the favour of gods who could not help them when help was most needed.

Rule out both a theophany and a prophet on the ground that either would certainly have been recorded, or else decline to specify the method at all and suggest that a stern experience may itself have spoken to the national conviction with a prophetic voice; turn the missing record of certain oppressions into a principle, that the narrative of the book is typical rather than exhaustive; suspect an early corruption behind one of the names, since the versions disagree, and canvass the possible towns before supposing the place was once the capital of a tribe that afterwards dwindled; defend a disputed particle against both manuscripts and versions; hear behind the dismissal the words of the song of Moses; and read the widening of the invasion as boldness bred by long success.

debates: By what means the Lord's answer was conveyed to the people.
Why no deliverance from the Zidonians and Maonites is recorded elsewhere.
Who the Maonites were, and whether the name is sound.
Whether a disputed particle belongs in the text of the confession.
outliers: Keil alone rules out both theophany and prophet, arguing from the silence of the record.
Ellicott alone proposes that experience itself was the prophetic voice, with no messenger at all.
Ellicott alone states the principle that the book's narrative is typical rather than exhaustive.
Keil alone defends the disputed particle against both the manuscripts and the versions.
Gill alone affirms the unrecorded oppressions as beyond question.

13.pericope_label: The gods ye have chosen, the putting away of the idols, and the muster at Mizpeh

schools.summary: Make the refusal to deliver a conditional threat, as such threats are elsewhere, which the sequel proves; answer the harder difficulty that God is said to change his mind by holding that the change of purpose implies no changeableness in the divine nature, concerning only his attitude towards his people; call the summons to the chosen gods a bitter reproach and set beside it the mockery on Carmel; hear behind it the older warning that they would be sent to the gods they chose; make the timing the point, that the moment sincerity was proved God hears them; gloss the divine grief literally as a shortening of the soul, or read it as impatience, since he could no longer look on the misery and was obliged to help; give the literal sense of the mustering as a crying together; identify the camp as the Mizpeh in Gilead, the name being common since it means watch-tower; and object that though there is no conjunction between the people and the princes they cannot stand in apposition, the word for people never being applied to princes.

Take the summons to the chosen gods as ironical and not serious, since it was never in their power to relieve; take the putting away of the idols for evidence of the truth of the repentance, showing the confessions and humiliations genuine; and reconstruct the movement of the invaders, who having crossed the river and distressed three tribes were told by a herald that the Israelites on the further side had risen in defence of their country and liberties, and so came back and crossed again.

Grant that the reprehension was kind, pointed and solemn, the repentance deep, and the proof of it genuine in the putting away of all the idols — then add that they were ever fickle and uncertain; take the divine grief as far as it will go, as a proof of the philanthropy of God, whose compassions move here on a small scale but by the same principle that gave his Son for the sins of the whole world; suppose criers sent out in different directions to stir up all the enemies of Israel; and observe that the people had no general, that in those times much depended on the onset since a war was generally decided in one battle, and that when God purposes to deliver he will in the course of his providence find out and direct the proper means.

debates: Whether the refusal to deliver again was absolute or conditional.
What the grieving of God's soul says about his nature.
How the people and the princes are related in the closing verse.
outliers: Ellicott alone declares the threat conditional; Keil alone answers the difficulty by distinguishing God's nature from his attitude.
Clarke alone extends the divine grief to the gift of the Son and the redemption of the world.
Clarke alone qualifies the repentance as genuine but fickle.
Gill alone reconstructs the recrossing of Jordan as a response to the herald's news.
